

# Machine Learning-Assisted Prediction and Operating-Window Identification for HPHT Energised Foam Rheology

# Proposal Summary

Hydraulic fracturing operations in high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) reservoirs require stable energised foams with predictable rheological behaviour to ensure effective proppant transport and fracture conductivity. However, conventional empirical approaches are constrained by limited experimental data, complex nonlinear fluid behaviour, and the absence of reliable methods for identifying optimal operating conditions.

This research proposes an uncertainty-aware machine learning framework to predict the rheological properties of HPHT energised foams and identify engineering operating windows for hydraulic fracturing-fluid design.

The study integrates experimental data compilation, predictive modelling, uncertainty quantification, optimisation, and engineering assessment within a petroleum engineering research methodology. Machine learning serves as a decision-support tool rather than the primary focus, ensuring that engineering judgement remains central throughout the investigation.

The expected outcome is a robust predictive framework that improves engineering decision-making, supports hydraulic fracturing-fluid formulation under HPHT conditions, and provides a foundation for future laboratory validation and field-scale application, thereby contributing to both petroleum engineering practice and research

# 2. Background and Petroleum Engineering Context

The performance of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams under HPHT conditions depends on complex interactions between reservoir conditions, fluid formulation, rheological behaviour, and engineering requirements. Understanding these relationships provides the foundation for evaluating their application in hydraulic fracturing and identifying the limitations that motivate this research.

## 2.1 Hydraulic Fracturing and the Role of Energised Foams

The exploitation of unconventional reservoirs and mature fields presents operational and environmental challenges for conventional water-based hydraulic fracturing. Water-based stimulation requires substantial volumes of freshwater, while fluid invasion may contribute to clay swelling and formation damage, potentially reducing reservoir productivity in water-sensitive formations (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022). Consequently, energised fracturing foams incorporating compressible gases such as nitrogen or carbon dioxide have emerged as alternative fluids for water-sensitive and under-pressured reservoirs (Wanniarachchi et al., 2017).

Energised foams can reduce water consumption while providing rheological properties that support proppant suspension and transport (Fei et al., 2018; Yekeen et al., 2018). Their engineering performance, however, depends strongly on maintaining suitable apparent viscosity and foam stability during fluid preparation, pumping, fracture propagation, and proppant placement. These properties are sensitive to interacting factors including pressure, temperature, foam quality, shear conditions, salinity, and chemical formulation. The principal engineering challenge is therefore not merely to generate a stable foam under controlled laboratory conditions, but to understand and predict how its rheological and stability characteristics change across the demanding and dynamic conditions of HPHT fracturing operations.

## 2.2 Foam Rheology under HPHT Conditions

The rheological behaviour of energised foams is strongly influenced by pressure, temperature, and shear conditions. These factors affect bubble structure, liquid drainage, apparent viscosity, and foam stability. Jing et al. (2019), for example, showed that increasing pressure alters gas-phase behaviour and bubble size, with corresponding effects on foam viscosity. Elevated temperatures have also been associated with faster liquid drainage and reduced viscosity and stability (Hutchins and Miller, 2005; Fu and Liu, 2021).

Although these studies provide important insights, their findings are often specific to particular formulations and experimental conditions. Fu and Liu (2021) and Lv et al. (2015), for example, examined foam behaviour at temperatures up to approximately 72°C and 90°C, respectively. While valuable, these experimental ranges do not capture the more extreme temperatures or the full range of coupled pressure and temperature conditions that may be encountered in HPHT reservoirs, which have been classified in previous literature as having temperatures above 150°C and pressures exceeding 69 MPa (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022). Similarly, studies that vary pressure or temperature independently may not fully capture how these variables interact with foam quality, shear rate, salinity, and chemical formulation under reservoir conditions (Sinha et al., 2019).

The literature therefore establishes that operating conditions strongly influence foam rheology and stability, but the evidence remains fragmented across different formulations, experimental methods, and operating ranges. This limits direct comparison between studies and makes it difficult to generalise observed relationships across broader HPHT fracturing conditions.

## 2.3 Foam Quality and Rheological Models

Foam quality, expressed as the volumetric gas fraction, strongly influences foam structure and rheological behaviour. Increasing foam quality can increase apparent viscosity up to a critical range, beyond which rheological behaviour may change as the foam structure becomes increasingly gas-dominated (Akhtar et al., 2018). To describe the resulting non-Newtonian and shear-thinning behaviour, studies have applied rheological models such as the Power-law, Bingham plastic, and Herschel–Bulkley equations (Ahmed et al., 2017).

Although these models provide useful representations of foam behaviour within their calibration ranges, their empirical parameters may not remain transferable across different formulations and operating conditions. The complex and heterogeneous structure of high-quality foams further complicates representation using simplified constitutive relationships (Princen and Kiss, 1989). More recently, machine learning approaches, including XGBoost and Artificial Neural Networks, have been applied to capture nonlinear relationships in foam rheological data (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024). However, where the models examined provide only deterministic point predictions, uncertainty arising from sparse data, experimental variability, and extrapolation beyond the training range remains unquantified. This limits confidence in their application to engineering decisions under variable HPHT conditions (Zhang et al., 2025).

## 2.4 Nanoparticle–Surfactant Interactions

To improve foam stability under elevated temperatures, silica nanoparticles have been used to form interfacial barriers that enhance film elasticity and delay liquid drainage (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022). Their stabilisation efficiency, however, depends strongly on interactions with the selected surfactant. For instance, combining negatively charged silica nanoparticles with cationic surfactants such as CTAB can induce strong electrostatic attraction, producing nanoparticle aggregates or “corks” that obstruct drainage channels (Tran et al., 2023). Studies have also reported higher apparent viscosity and stability for some cationic surfactant–nanoparticle systems than for comparable anionic mixtures (Tran et al., 2025).

This stabilising effect is highly concentration-dependent. Tran et al. (2022) reported that exceeding an optimal cationic surfactant concentration can induce excessive nanoparticle flocculation, causing particles to remain or precipitate in the bulk phase rather than stabilising the interface, with a corresponding decline in foam stability. These nonlinear and formulation-specific interactions create an important predictive challenge because relationships observed within one concentration range may not remain valid beyond it. Accurately identifying such thresholds is therefore important for predicting foam performance and defining candidate operating windows.

## 2.5 Proppant Transport and Engineering Performance

The effective suspension and transport of proppant into the fracture network are important engineering functions of energised fracturing foams. Compared with conventional slickwater, foams can provide rheological and elastic properties that support improved proppant suspension and distribution under certain conditions (Fei et al., 2018). Proppant settling is also influenced by fluid viscosity, making the maintenance of suitable rheological behaviour important for effective transport (Goel et al., 2002).

A critical limitation, however, is that elevated temperatures can degrade foam stability and compromise proppant suspension. Lv et al. (2015), for example, reported substantial increases in proppant settling velocity under elevated-temperature conditions. Because proppant transport is a downstream engineering consequence influenced by foam rheology and stability, uncertainty in predicting these primary properties may propagate into subsequent assessments of proppant behaviour and fracture performance (Tran et al., 2025). This reinforces the need to quantify predictive uncertainty when identifying candidate operating windows for further laboratory and engineering evaluation.

## 2.6 Critical Synthesis of the Existing Literature

The literature has established important relationships between HPHT conditions, foam quality, nanoparticle–surfactant interactions, rheological behaviour, and proppant transport (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022; Tran et al., 2025). Conventional rheological models provide useful descriptions within defined experimental conditions (Ahmed et al., 2017), while data-driven approaches offer additional capacity to capture complex nonlinear relationships (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024). However, the evidence remains fragmented across different formulations, experimental methods, operating ranges, and measured outputs, limiting direct comparison and broader generalisation.

This fragmentation is compounded by small, formulation-specific datasets and limited coverage of coupled HPHT conditions (Sinha et al., 2019). As a result, models calibrated or trained on particular datasets may perform well within the conditions represented but provide limited evidence of reliability under sparse, unfamiliar, or extrapolated conditions. Where predictions are deterministic, uncertainty arising from experimental variability, limited data coverage, and model limitations may also remain unquantified (Ogbidi and Oteh, 2023).

The central challenge is therefore not simply the limited application of uncertainty-aware machine learning to foam rheology. Rather, existing approaches do not yet adequately integrate HPHT foam behaviour, predictive uncertainty, and engineering interpretation within a framework capable of supporting candidate operating-window identification. Addressing this limitation is important because fracturing-fluid design requires not only predictions of apparent viscosity and foam stability, but also an understanding of their reliability and implications for downstream engineering assessment (Tran et al., 2025).

# 3. Research Problem

Hydraulic fracturing operations in High-Pressure, High-Temperature (HPHT) reservoirs increasingly utilise energised foams to reduce water consumption, minimise formation damage, and support proppant transport (Wanniarachchi et al., 2017; Fei et al., 2018). Despite these advantages, maintaining suitable foam performance under HPHT conditions remains a significant engineering challenge. Elevated temperatures and pressures can influence liquid drainage, bubble coalescence, gas diffusion, and other physicochemical processes that alter foam rheology and stability (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022).

Predicting this behaviour is difficult because apparent viscosity and foam stability are governed by coupled, nonlinear interactions among pressure, temperature, foam quality, surfactant chemistry, nanoparticle concentration, salinity, shear rate, and gas-phase characteristics (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024; Ghorbani, 2025). Consequently, a foam formulation that performs adequately under one set of experimental or operating conditions may not exhibit the same behaviour under different HPHT conditions.

The core engineering problem is therefore not simply that energised foam rheology is difficult to predict. Unreliable prediction of apparent viscosity and foam stability can compromise fracturing-fluid formulation and the identification of suitable operating conditions, with downstream implications for proppant suspension and transport, fracture conductivity, and overall treatment performance (Tran et al., 2025). Without sufficiently reliable predictions and an understanding of their uncertainty, engineers have limited confidence in determining how nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams will perform across variable HPHT conditions. This creates a need for a predictive approach that can model the primary rheological and stability characteristics of these foams while assessing the reliability of its predictions to support fracturing-fluid design and subsequent engineering evaluation.

# 4. Knowledge Gap and Significance

## 4.1 Knowledge Gap

Empirical and mechanistic models, including the Power-law, Bingham plastic, and Carreau models, have long been used to represent the rheological behaviour of energised foams under controlled experimental conditions (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024; Ghorbani, 2025). Although these models provide valuable insights into apparent viscosity and yield behaviour, their parameters and simplifying assumptions may not remain transferable across the coupled nonlinear interactions among pressure, temperature, shear rate, foam quality, surfactant chemistry, nanoparticle concentration, salinity, and gas-phase characteristics encountered under HPHT conditions. This limits confidence in their generalisation across different formulations and operating environments (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022).

Recent studies have increasingly applied machine learning techniques, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and Artificial Neural Networks, to capture nonlinear relationships and predict foam rheological properties (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024; Ghassemzadeh et al., 2021). However, the available studies rely predominantly on laboratory-scale and formulation-specific datasets, with limited representation of diverse and coupled HPHT conditions. Their predictive performance is therefore closely tied to the conditions represented in the available data. Where models provide only deterministic point predictions, uncertainty arising from sparse data, experimental variability, and extrapolation beyond the training range remains unquantified.

Uncertainty quantification has been applied in other areas of petroleum engineering, including reservoir characterisation and production forecasting (Ogbidi and Oteh, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), but its integration with predictive modelling of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foam rheology remains limited. Consequently, existing approaches provide limited information about prediction reliability under sparse, unfamiliar, or extrapolated HPHT conditions. This matters because uncertainty in predicted apparent viscosity and foam stability may affect the identification of suitable formulation and operating ranges and subsequent engineering assessments of proppant suspension and transport.

The limitations identified across existing rheological, experimental, and data-driven approaches are synthesised in the Critical Gap Matrix presented in Table 4.1.

As shown in Table 4.1, the research gap is not attributable to a single methodological limitation, but to the lack of integration between HPHT-relevant data, nonlinear prediction, uncertainty quantification, and engineering interpretation.

## 4.2 Significance of the Research

Therefore, a significant scientific and engineering gap remains. Existing empirical, mechanistic, and data-driven approaches have not yet adequately integrated heterogeneous HPHT foam data, nonlinear prediction of apparent viscosity and foam stability, explicit uncertainty quantification, and engineering interpretation within a coherent framework. Addressing this gap requires an uncertainty-aware predictive framework capable of assessing model reliability across variable HPHT conditions and supporting candidate operating-window identification for further laboratory and engineering evaluation. Such a framework could support fracturing-fluid design by providing not only predictions of foam behaviour, but also an indication of the confidence and limitations associated with those predictions.

# 5. Aim, Objectives, and Research Questions

## 5.1 Aim

The primary aim of this doctoral research is to develop an uncertainty-aware predictive framework to support High-Pressure, High-Temperature (HPHT) energised foam design, utilising machine learning to predict apparent viscosity and stability, quantify uncertainty, and identify safe operating windows for hydraulic fracturing applications**.**

## 5.2 Research Questions

To achieve this aim, the research seeks to address the following technical questions:

1. Which formulation and operating variables most strongly control the apparent viscosity and foam stability of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams under HPHT conditions?
2. How accurately can machine learning models predict apparent viscosity and foam stability across varying pressure, temperature, salinity, foam quality, and chemical formulation conditions?
3. How can prediction uncertainty be quantified and incorporated into the interpretation of foam rheology models?
4. How can uncertainty-aware predictions support operating-window identification for fracturing-fluid design and proppant transport assessment?

## 5.3 Research Objectives

The objectives of this research align directly with the research questions and the proposed methodology. Each objective is designed to yield a clear engineering deliverable:

To investigate the influence of pressure, temperature, fluid composition, and shear conditions on the rheological behaviour of energized foams under HPHT reservoir conditions.

1. Compile and structure HPHT foam rheology and stability datasets from available experimental and literature sources.
2. Develop and compare selected ML models for predicting apparent viscosity and foam stability indicators.
3. Quantify prediction uncertainty and assess model reliability under sparse or extrapolated HPHT conditions.
4. Identify operating windows for nanoparticle-stabilised energised foam formulations under defined reservoir and treatment constraints.
5. Evaluate the engineering implications of the model outputs for fracturing-fluid design and proppant transport

# 6. Proposed Methodology

## 6.1 Introduction

This research proposes a data-driven workflow to predict and evaluate the rheological behaviour of nanoparticle-stabilised energised fracturing foams under High-Pressure, High-Temperature (HPHT) reservoir conditions (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022). Rather than replacing physical engineering judgment, the machine learning frameworks proposed in this study are expected to serve strictly as advanced decision-support tools (Ghassemzadeh et al., 2021; Ogbidi and Oteh, 2023). The methodology is systematically designed to address complex petroleum parameters, integrating predictive analytics with the petroleum engineering assessment of foam stability, proppant suspension, and ultimate fracture conductivity (Fei et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2025).

## 6.2 Proposed Methodology Overview

To ensure methodological rigour and maintain the petroleum engineering focus of this study, the proposed methodology is presented through a series of complementary conceptual and methodological frameworks rather than a purely descriptive narrative. The use of multiple visual frameworks improves the communication of complex research designs by illustrating the logical relationships between the research problem, objectives, methodology, and expected outcomes, thereby enhancing transparency, coherence, and reproducibility (Maxwell, 2013; Creswell and Creswell, 2023).

This layered presentation also enables the reader to understand the progression of the research from problem identification to engineering application while demonstrating how machine learning is integrated as a supporting analytical tool within an engineering-led investigation.

## 6.2.1 Conceptual Framework of the Research Methodology

This subsection presents the conceptual frameworks underpinning the proposed research methodology. Rather than representing independent models, the four frameworks provide complementary perspectives of the study, illustrating the progression from problem identification and methodological alignment to engineering workflow and predictive model implementation. Together, they establish the conceptual foundation for the five engineering modules described in Sections 6.3–6.7.

To operationalise the proposed research methodology, the study is structured into five interconnected engineering modules, namely Data Compilation and Preparation (Section 6.3), Rheology and Stability Prediction (Section 6.4), Uncertainty Quantification (Section 6.5), Operating-Window Identification (Section 6.6), and Engineering Assessment (Section 6.7). This iterative stage-gate approach enhances transparency, reproducibility, and engineering rigour while ensuring that predictive modelling remains embedded within an engineering-led research framework**.**

## 6.3 Data Compilation and Preparation

Because HPHT foam datasets are typically sparse, formulation-specific, and rarely formatted for computational modelling, this initial methodological module implements a targeted data extraction strategy to support project feasibility (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024).

**Objective:** To compile, extract, and standardise HPHT foam rheology and stability datasets suitable for predictive modelling.

**Inputs:** Published experimental studies, publicly available datasets, supplementary materials associated with published research, and laboratory datasets where available (Tran et al., 2023; Tran et al., 2025).

**Activities:** Data will be harvested primarily from peer-reviewed published studies and structured into a multi-variable feature matrix (Table 6.1). These specific variables were strategically selected because they collectively govern the operational, physicochemical, and rheological behaviour of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams under extreme HPHT conditions (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022; Al-Darweesh et al., 2024). To resolve inconsistencies across different independent experimental studies, rigorous dataset standardisation protocols will be applied where appropriate (Table 6.2).

**Outputs:** A harmonised, quality-assured dataset suitable for predictive modelling.

**Decision Point:** Does the harmonised dataset meet the predefined quality criteria for model development? If No, augment the dataset through additional data acquisition, improve the preprocessing procedures where necessary, and repeat the compilation and standardisation workflow. If Yes, proceed to Section 6.4: Rheology and Stability Prediction.

|Foam Half-life|Output|min|Primary predictive stability target|Measures foam stability under HPHT conditions|\|   \|<br>\|---\|<br>\|<br><br>\|   \|<br>\|---\|<br>\|Tran et al. (2022); Gonzalez Perdomo & Wan Madihi (2022)\||
|Drainage Rate|Output|%|Secondary foam stability indicator|Evaluates liquid drainage and foam decay|Tran et al. (2022); Fu & Liu (2021)|

The feature matrix presented in Table 6.1 defines the proposed input and output variables that will form the foundation of the predictive modelling framework. These variables capture the principal operational, physicochemical, and engineering factors influencing HPHT energised foam behaviour and provide a structured basis for subsequent data compilation and feature engineering. However, because these data are expected to be compiled from multiple independent experimental studies, additional preprocessing is required to ensure consistency before model development.

Following variable selection, the compiled datasets will undergo the standardisation procedures summarised in Table 6.2 to minimise inconsistencies arising from differences in reporting formats, measurement units, terminology, and experimental protocols. These preprocessing activities are intended to improve data quality and ensure that the harmonised dataset is suitable for reliable machine learning analysis and subsequent engineering interpretation.

**Table 6.2   Dataset Standardisation Protocol**

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|**Data Issue**|**Standardisation Strategy**|**Key References**|
|Variable pressure/temperature units|Uniform conversion to MPa and °C|Gonzalez Perdomo & Wan Madihi (2022); Tran et al. (2023)|
|Variable chemical concentration units|Uniform conversion to weight percentage (wt%)|Tran et al. (2022); Tran et al. (2023)|
|Missing experimental metadata|Statistical imputation where appropriate, or record removal|Géron (2023); Kuhn & Johnson (2019)|
|Duplicate observations|Remove duplicate records|Géron (2023); Kuhn & Johnson (2019)|
|Inconsistent measurement scales|Z-score normalisation or Min-Max scaling|Géron (2023); Kuhn & Johnson (2019)|
|Experimental outliers|Statistical anomaly detection coupled with physical engineering review|Géron (2023); Kuhn & Johnson (2019)|
|Inconsistent terminology|Harmonisation of variable names across disparate studies|Tran et al. (2023); Al-Darweesh et al. (2024)|

The procedures are intended to improve data consistency, comparability, and suitability for subsequent machine learning analysis._

Once the dataset has been compiled and standardised, appropriate analytical methods will be selected to develop, compare, and evaluate predictive models. Because the compiled HPHT dataset is expected to exhibit nonlinear relationships, varying data density, and potential uncertainty, multiple complementary machine learning approaches are proposed rather than relying on a single algorithm. The rationale for selecting these analytical methods is summarised in Table 6.3.

|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Method**|**Primary Purpose**|**Justification for Selection**|**Expected Output**|**Key References**|

|Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)|Improve predictive accuracy for complex nonlinear relationships|Efficient gradient boosting algorithm capable of modelling complex interactions among pressure, temperature, foam quality, surfactant concentration, nanoparticle concentration, and other variables while maintaining strong predictive performance.|Enhanced deterministic predictions and comparative model performance.|Chen & Guestrin (2016); Géron (2023)|

The analytical methods presented in Table 6.3 represent a progressive modelling strategy, beginning with robust baseline algorithms and extending to probabilistic approaches capable of quantifying predictive uncertainty. The final selection of models will depend on the characteristics of the compiled dataset and their demonstrated predictive performance. The implementation and evaluation of these methods are described in the following section on Rheology and Stability Prediction.

## 6.4 Rheology and Stability Prediction

This module addresses the complex fluid dynamics of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams as they transition from near-Newtonian to highly non-Newtonian, shear-thinning behaviour under varying HPHT shear conditions (Ghorbani, 2025).

**Objective:** To systematically develop and evaluate predictive models capable of mapping the nonlinear rheological behaviour and stability profiles of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams under HPHT conditions.

**Inputs:** The harmonised dataset generated in Section 6.3.

**Activities:** To prevent unnecessary algorithmic complexity and ensure strict scope control, this phase adopts a staged modelling strategy. Initial evaluations will begin with robust and interpretable baseline models, such as Random Forest and XGBoost, to establish baseline predictive performance and investigate the coupled effects of pressure, temperature, and fluid composition (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024). Where dataset size and quality permit, more complex architectures such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) may also be evaluated to determine whether additional predictive performance can be achieved without significant overfitting.

Model validation will not rely solely on random point-wise splitting, as measurements from the same formulation or experimental study may be highly correlated and could overestimate predictive performance. Where permitted by the size and structure of the compiled dataset, grouped validation will therefore be applied by withholding complete formulations, experimental studies, or defined operating ranges. This will test model generalisation across unseen formulations, data sources, and HPHT conditions. Interpolation within the training domain will be distinguished from extrapolation beyond the ranges represented in the training data, with out-of-domain predictions evaluated separately and subsequently interpreted alongside the uncertainty estimates generated in Section 6.5. Random train/test splitting may be retained as a baseline comparison rather than the sole evidence of model generalisation.

Model performance will be evaluated using appropriate regression metrics, including Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²).

**Outputs:** Validated deterministic predictions of the primary targets, apparent viscosity and foam half-life together with evidence of model performance and generalisation across the evaluated validation scenarios.

**Decision Point:** Does the selected predictive model satisfy the predefined performance and validation criteria for reliable engineering prediction? If No, revise the feature engineering process, optimise the model specification, and repeat the model development and validation workflow. If Yes, proceed to Section 6.5 – Predictive Uncertainty Quantification.

## 6.5 Predictive Uncertainty Quantification

Current deterministic approaches applied to fracturing fluids output rigid point-predictions, often neglecting the underlying physical measurement sparsity typical of HPHT laboratory datasets. This module directly addresses that critical engineering limitation.

**Objective:** To incorporate uncertainty quantification into the predictive framework by estimating confidence intervals for the rheological predictions and supporting more reliable engineering interpretation.

**Inputs:** The best-performing predictive model(s) identified during the rheology and stability prediction stage (Section 6.4).

**Activities:** Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) will be applied exclusively to the models demonstrating the highest baseline accuracy. Crucially, this phase will explicitly decouple aleatoric uncertainty (arising from inherent experimental measurement noise and fluid variability) from epistemic uncertainty (arising from sparse laboratory data and model limitations) (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). Depending on the characteristics of the compiled dataset, appropriate uncertainty quantification techniques, including Bayesian inference, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), or ensemble-based prediction intervals (e.g., Monte Carlo Dropout), will be evaluated to determine the most suitable approach for estimating predictive uncertainty (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016; Ogbidi and Oteh, 2023). The candidate uncertainty quantification methods will be compared based on their calibration performance, interval reliability, predictive accuracy, and practical usefulness for supporting petroleum engineering decision-making. The method demonstrating the most appropriate balance between predictive performance, uncertainty reliability, and engineering applicability will be adopted for subsequent operating-window identification.

**Outputs:** Uncertainty-aware predictions, confidence intervals, and quantitative measures of predictive uncertainty for apparent viscosity and foam stability

**Decision Point:** Do the uncertainty estimates satisfy the predefined confidence requirements for engineering decision-making? If No, improve the predictive model and recalibrate the uncertainty quantification approach before repeating the assessment. If Yes, proceed to Section 6.6: Operating Window Identification and Engineering Optimisation.

## 6.6 Operating Window Identification

To translate uncertainty-aware predictions into practical engineering guidance, this module identifies the operational conditions under which nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams are expected to achieve acceptable engineering performance while maintaining acceptable predictive uncertainty.

**Objective:** To identify multidimensional candidate operating windows within which nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams are predicted to achieve acceptable engineering performance while maintaining acceptable predictive uncertainty for hydraulic fracturing-fluid design.

**Inputs:** Uncertainty-aware predictions of apparent viscosity and foam stability, together with the associated uncertainty estimates generated in Section 6.5.

**Activities:** Appropriate optimisation techniques, including Bayesian Optimisation where suitable, will be evaluated to support operating-window identification (Shahriari et al., 2016). Within this study, an operating window is defined as the multidimensional range of pressure, temperature, foam quality, salinity, surfactant concentration, nanoparticle concentration, and related operational variables within which nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams are predicted to achieve acceptable apparent viscosity, foam stability, and proppant-support capability while maintaining acceptable predictive uncertainty for hydraulic fracturing-fluid design. The acceptance criteria and engineering constraints will be informed by relevant experimental evidence, literature, and available design requirements. This definition establishes the operating window as an engineering decision-support tool rather than simply an optimisation outcome (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022).

**Outputs:** Uncertainty-bounded candidate operating windows and proposed operational ranges to support hydraulic fracturing-fluid formulation and subsequent engineering assessment.

**Decision Point:** Do the identified candidate operating windows satisfy the predefined engineering requirements for HPHT hydraulic fracturing-fluid design? If No, revise the optimisation framework, review the predictive modelling outputs, and repeat the operating window identification process. If Yes, proceed to Section 6.7: Engineering Assessment.

## 6.7 Engineering assessment

This final module evaluates how the uncertainty-aware predictive framework can support petroleum engineering decision-making by relating the predicted rheological behaviour and identified operating windows to hydraulic fracturing-fluid performance under HPHT reservoir conditions.

**Objective:** To evaluate how the predicted rheological behaviour and identified operating windows can support engineering assessment of hydraulic fracturing-fluid performance under HPHT conditions.

**Inputs:** The proposed operating windows, predicted rheological properties, and associated uncertainty estimates generated in Section 6.6.

**Activities:** The engineering assessment will integrate the predicted rheological behaviour, uncertainty estimates, and identified operating windows to evaluate their practical relevance for hydraulic fracturing-fluid design under HPHT conditions. The assessment will examine predicted rheological performance, foam stability, proppant transport capability, and fracture conductivity in relation to published experimental evidence and established engineering principles (Tran et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2018). The operational feasibility of the identified operating windows will also be evaluated by considering predictive uncertainty, engineering constraints, and practical design requirements. Finally, the assessment will identify engineering trade-offs, discuss the assumptions and limitations of the proposed predictive framework, and highlight areas requiring further laboratory validation before potential field application.

**Outputs:** Engineering assessment of the proposed predictive framework, design recommendations for HPHT hydraulic fracturing-fluid formulation, identified engineering limitations, and recommendations for future validation and field application.

**Decision Point:** Does the proposed framework demonstrate sufficient engineering validity to support hydraulic fracturing-fluid design and operational decision-making? If No, strengthen the predictive framework, revise the engineering assessment, and repeat the evaluation. If Yes, proceed to 7 – Data Requirements and Feasibility.

# 7 Data Requirements and Feasibility

Given the limited availability, size, heterogeneity, and structure of HPHT foam rheology and stability datasets, this research adopts a realistic data strategy that prioritises accessible sources and avoids dependence on proprietary or otherwise unavailable data.

This research acknowledges that HPHT foam rheology and stability datasets in the existing literature are frequently small, formulation-specific, heterogeneous, and rarely reported in a format directly suitable for machine learning applications (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024). Consequently, the primary data strategy will begin with available published experimental datasets and the systematic extraction, structuring, digitisation, and standardisation of relevant HPHT foam measurements (Tran et al., 2023). Publicly available datasets and supplementary research materials will be incorporated where suitable. Research-group datasets will be considered only where they are available, relevant, and appropriately approved for use.

The computational modelling strategy will be adapted to the size, quality, structure, and variable coverage of the resulting master dataset. Selected machine learning and uncertainty quantification methods will be evaluated based on the available data characteristics, with model complexity restricted where data availability is insufficient to support more complex model architectures (Ogbidi and Oteh, 2023).

Ultimately, the feasibility of subsequent predictive modelling will be assessed on the basis of dataset adequacy rather than assumed in advance. If the compiled dataset is deemed insufficient in terms of size, completeness, variable coverage, or experimental diversity, the data search and extraction strategy will be broadened, and the modelling scope will be adjusted to align with the available physical evidence.

# 8. Expected Contributions

This research is expected to contribute to petroleum engineering through the data-driven prediction and engineering assessment of nanoparticle-stabilised energised fracturing foams under HPHT conditions. The expected contributions are aligned with the research objectives and proposed methodology.

**8.1 Structured HPHT Foam Data Resource**

Through the systematic extraction, digitisation, harmonisation, and standardisation of available experimental data, the research is expected to produce a structured dataset and reproducible data-preparation approach for the analysis of heterogeneous HPHT foam rheology and stability data.

**8.2 Predictive Framework for HPHT Foam Rheology and Stability**

The study is expected to develop and evaluate a data-driven framework for predicting the apparent viscosity and foam stability of nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams across varying formulation and HPHT operating conditions.

**8.3 Uncertainty Quantification and Model Reliability Assessment**

The research is expected to extend deterministic prediction by quantifying predictive uncertainty and assessing model reliability under sparse and extrapolated HPHT conditions. This will provide a basis for interpreting model predictions with greater awareness of their confidence and limitations.

**8.4 Candidate Operating-Window Identification**

The study is expected to identify uncertainty-bounded candidate operating windows representing combinations of pressure, temperature, foam quality, salinity, surfactant concentration, and nanoparticle concentration associated with acceptable rheological and stability performance under defined engineering constraints.

**8.5 Engineering Assessment for Fracturing-Fluid Design**

The research is expected to evaluate the implications of predicted foam rheology, stability, and candidate operating windows for fracturing-fluid design and the downstream assessment of proppant suspension and transport. This assessment will connect the predictive outputs to relevant petroleum engineering considerations without treating the models as substitutes for experimental validation or engineering judgement.

Collectively, these contributions are expected to provide an uncertainty-aware predictive framework for estimating apparent viscosity and foam stability, quantifying prediction uncertainty, and identifying candidate operating windows for nanoparticle-stabilised energised foams under HPHT conditions. The resulting outputs are intended to support further laboratory and engineering evaluation rather than provide automatically field-ready design decisions.

# 9. Scope and Limitations

This research is bounded to the evaluation and prediction of nanoparticle-stabilised energised fracturing foams under HPHT conditions. In direct alignment with the research objectives, a clear distinction is maintained between primary predictive targets and downstream engineering applications. The machine learning framework is scoped to predict apparent viscosity and foam stability, operationalised primarily through foam half-life, as the central predictive targets (Gonzalez Perdomo and Wan Madihi, 2022). Proppant transport assessment and operating-window identification are treated as downstream engineering applications informed by these predictions (Tran et al., 2025).

While the study will evaluate the engineering implications of foam rheology and stability for proppant suspension and transport, it will not attempt to develop a fully coupled three-dimensional hydraulic fracturing simulator. Instead, the framework will identify uncertainty-bounded candidate operating windows to support further laboratory evaluation, engineering assessment, and existing fracture-design workflows. The empirical modelling is also constrained by the availability, size, heterogeneity, variable coverage, and formulation specificity of accessible HPHT foam rheology and stability datasets (Al-Darweesh et al., 2024).

# 10. Alignment with My Background

This proposed research sits at the intersection of predictive analytics, engineering systems, and petroleum engineering. My academic background, which includes a Master of Research in Artificial Intelligence with Distinction, provides a strong foundation in Bayesian optimisation, uncertainty quantification, and time-series data modelling. These capabilities are relevant to the computational components of the proposed research, particularly the prediction of foam rheology and stability, assessment of model uncertainty, and identification of candidate operating windows.

Professionally, my experience as a Research Assistant on a UKRI-funded Knowledge Transfer Partnership, where I contributed to the development of IoT-enabled predictive monitoring systems for high-pressure subsea hydraulic networks, provides relevant experience in analysing complex engineering systems involving pressure, operating variability, monitoring, and uncertainty. Although this experience is not equivalent to petroleum engineering or hydraulic fracturing-fluid design, it provides a transferable engineering systems perspective for investigating fluid behaviour and predictive performance under demanding operating conditions. My membership of the Society of Petroleum Engineers (SPE) further reflects my ongoing engagement with the petroleum and energy sector.

At the same time, I recognise that petroleum engineering, foam rheology, and hydraulic fracturing-fluid design are specialised areas in which I will need to deepen my knowledge during the early stages of candidature. My existing strengths lie primarily in artificial intelligence, predictive modelling, uncertainty quantification, and engineering systems. The doctoral programme will therefore require deliberate development of the domain-specific knowledge needed to apply these capabilities appropriately to nanoparticle-stabilised energised foam systems under HPHT conditions.

This interdisciplinary development is an important part of the proposed research and will help ensure that the computational methods are informed by relevant physical principles, experimental evidence, and petroleum engineering judgement.
